purpose: A received history of the computer becoming a digital medium: from programmable symbolic machinery through interactive graphics, personal creative tools, networked publishing, games, social and streaming platforms, and generative or agentic media. Events are selected for their influence on representation, interaction, authorship, distribution, participation, and cultural use rather than hardware performance alone.
sourceNote: The chronology synthesizes reputable secondary histories and museum timelines, checked against well-established release records and research summaries where useful. It is intended as a sound basis for counterfactual and future scenario construction, not as original priority research.

events.label: Turing's Universal Machine
events.description: Alan Turing describes a single abstract machine able to execute any computable symbolic procedure, establishing programmability as a general medium rather than a feature of one purpose-built calculator.

events.label: Von Neumann's EDVAC Report
events.description: The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC describes instructions and data held in the same memory, circulating the stored-program architecture that lets computers change purpose through software.

events.label: ENIAC
events.description: ENIAC demonstrates large-scale general electronic computation at unprecedented speed, although new programs initially require operators to reconfigure cables and switches by hand.

events.label: Manchester Baby Runs a Stored Program
events.description: The Manchester Baby runs the first electronic program stored in a computer's working memory, turning the stored-program proposal into an operating machine.

events.label: Whirlwind and Real-Time Interaction
events.description: MIT's Whirlwind couples high-speed computation to a visual display and immediate input, helping establish the alternative to batch processing: a computer that responds while a person uses it.

events.label: UNIVAC Enters Business and Television
events.description: UNIVAC I becomes the first commercially produced US computer and gains public fame by predicting the 1952 presidential election on television, presenting computation as an information medium.

events.label: The ILLIAC Suite
events.description: Lejaren Hiller and Leonard Isaacson use the ILLIAC computer to compose a substantial musical score, making algorithmic generation part of the modern debate over creativity and authorship.

events.label: The First Scanned Digital Image
events.description: Russell Kirsch's team scans a photograph into the SEAC computer as a grid of numerical pixels, establishing the digital image as data that can be stored and transformed.

events.label: Spacewar!
events.description: MIT programmers create Spacewar! as a responsive audiovisual world for two players and freely circulate its code, making the computer itself a medium for play.

events.label: Sketchpad
events.description: Ivan Sutherland's Sketchpad lets a user draw and manipulate structured graphics directly with a light pen, introducing constraints, reusable objects, and direct-manipulation visual computing.

events.label: ELIZA
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA produces conversational responses through pattern matching; users nevertheless attribute understanding and personality to text generated by a program.

events.label: The Mother of All Demos
events.description: Douglas Engelbart demonstrates the mouse, windows, hypertext, collaborative editing, video conferencing, and networked knowledge work as parts of one interactive media environment.

events.label: ARPANET
events.description: ARPANET links remote research computers through packet switching, providing an experimental foundation for networked communication, shared resources, email, and the later internet.

events.label: Pong and the Video-Game Business
events.description: Atari's Pong turns a simple real-time screen interaction into a mass amusement business, helping establish video games as a durable commercial medium.

events.label: SuperPaint
events.description: Richard Shoup's Xerox PARC system combines a frame buffer, drawing tools, color graphics, animation, and video input, anticipating paint software and digital video production.

events.label: The Xerox Alto
events.description: The Alto integrates a bitmap display, mouse, overlapping graphical elements, files, fonts, and network access into the recognizable model of a personal graphical computer.

events.label: Ethernet
events.description: Robert Metcalfe and colleagues design Ethernet to connect personal computers, printers, and servers inside the office, making local networked media practical.

events.label: Altair and the Homebrew Computer Club
events.description: The Altair 8800 and Homebrew Computer Club turn computing into a kit-building hobbyist culture where users exchange code, modify machines, and imagine computers as personal tools.

events.label: Apple II
events.description: The Apple II packages color graphics, sound, expansion, and approachable software in a consumer machine, bringing programming, games, education, and creative experimentation into homes.

events.label: The First Public Dial-Up BBS
events.description: Ward Christensen and Randy Suess launch CBBS, demonstrating that personal computers and telephone modems can support persistent public messages and user-run online communities.

events.label: VisiCalc
events.description: VisiCalc turns the spreadsheet into an interactive model whose visible values recalculate immediately, proving software could define why people bought a personal computer.

events.label: Usenet
events.description: Usenet distributes topic-based discussions across independently operated computers, creating a large participatory culture of pseudonyms, moderation norms, arguments, collaboration, and shared files.

events.label: Lucasfilm Computer Graphics Division
events.description: George Lucas recruits Ed Catmull to build a digital graphics group, joining computer science to film production and seeding Pixar and the modern visual-effects pipeline.

events.label: The IBM PC
events.description: IBM's modular PC and Microsoft's operating system create a widely cloned hardware-software standard, expanding personal computing while shifting control toward interoperable components and software vendors.

events.label: Commodore 64
events.description: Low price, retail distribution, color graphics, and a capable sound chip make the Commodore 64 a mass home medium for games, programming, music, and amateur production.

events.label: MIDI
events.description: The Musical Instrument Digital Interface standard lets electronic instruments and computers exchange performance instructions, reorganizing music composition, recording, and live production around editable data.

events.label: Apple Macintosh
events.description: The Macintosh brings the mouse-driven graphical interface, proportional type, and visual document creation to a mass audience, helping launch desktop publishing and design software.

events.label: Commodore Amiga
events.description: The Amiga combines advanced color graphics, sampled sound, animation, and video compatibility in an affordable computer, crystallizing the idea of the multimedia computer.

events.label: HyperCard
events.description: Apple's HyperCard lets non-specialists combine text, images, buttons, links, and scripts into shareable stacks, popularizing hypermedia and vernacular interactive authorship.

events.label: The World Wide Web
events.description: Tim Berners-Lee combines URLs, HTTP, HTML, a server, and a browser-editor into an open linked publishing system that can operate across the internet.

events.label: Adobe Photoshop
events.description: Photoshop makes layered digital image manipulation a standard professional and eventually popular practice, weakening the photograph's cultural association with an untouched record.

events.label: MP3 Compression
events.description: MPEG audio standards compress recorded sound into files small enough for practical network exchange, separating music distribution from physical carriers while intensifying copying conflicts.

events.label: Mosaic Browser
events.description: Mosaic's accessible graphical browser displays images within web pages and makes navigation straightforward, helping turn the Web from a specialist system into a popular visual medium.

events.label: Doom
events.description: Doom combines fast first-person 3D graphics, network play, shareware distribution, and user modification, establishing the game engine as both commercial medium and creative platform.

events.label: Netscape and the Commercial Web
events.description: Netscape Navigator and its spectacular public offering make the browser a strategic platform and signal that publishing, commerce, and media are moving onto the Web.

events.label: Toy Story
events.description: Pixar's Toy Story becomes the first fully computer-animated feature film, proving synthetic imagery can sustain mainstream characters, performance, visual style, and feature-length narrative.

events.label: JavaScript
events.description: JavaScript brings programmable behavior into the browser, gradually transforming web pages from linked documents into interactive applications, creative works, games, and media players.

events.label: Flash
events.description: FutureSplash and then Adobe Flash provide compact animation, sound, video, and scripting inside browsers, enabling a distinctive era of web cartoons, games, experiments, and streaming players.

events.label: Google Search
events.description: Google's link-based ranking makes an expanding Web navigable, then couples discovery to targeted advertising, turning search into a central mediator of visibility and media economics.

events.label: Napster
events.description: Napster makes searching and exchanging MP3 files effortless for millions, normalizing peer-to-peer music access while provoking lawsuits that reshape digital distribution and licensing.

events.label: Wikipedia
events.description: Wikipedia demonstrates that a large volunteer community using wiki software can continually produce and police a free reference work, challenging professional gatekeeping and fixed publication.

events.label: iPod and iTunes Store
events.description: Apple joins portable storage, library software, per-track purchasing, and record-label licensing into a managed digital music ecosystem, offering an industry-backed successor to file sharing.

events.label: Second Life
events.description: Second Life offers a persistent user-built world with avatars, scripting, property, and a convertible economy, making social presence and amateur world-making the content of a platform.

events.label: Podcasting
events.description: RSS enclosures and portable audio players let independent producers syndicate downloadable programs directly to subscribers; directories soon turn podcasting into a recognizable medium.

events.label: Facebook and the News Feed
events.description: Facebook organizes online identity around real-name social graphs, then News Feed turns friends' activities into an algorithmically ordered stream that users consume rather than deliberately visit.

events.label: YouTube
events.description: YouTube removes much of the friction from uploading, embedding, finding, and commenting on video, creating a global amateur archive and an advertising-supported creator economy.

events.label: Twitter
events.description: Twitter combines short public posts, following, hashtags, reposting, and real-time mobile use, becoming infrastructure for news, celebrity, activism, humor, harassment, and ambient awareness.

events.label: Netflix Begins Streaming
events.description: Netflix adds on-demand internet viewing to its DVD service, helping shift film and television from scheduled channels and physical media toward subscription libraries and data-driven commissioning.

events.label: The iPhone
events.description: The iPhone combines a multitouch computer, camera, media player, phone, and full web browser, making networked audiovisual creation and consumption an always-carried practice.

events.label: Apple App Store
events.description: The App Store turns mobile software into a centrally reviewed and revenue-shared marketplace, enabling vast creative experimentation while consolidating distribution, payment, and policy control.

events.label: Spotify
events.description: Spotify popularizes licensed, on-demand access to a vast music catalog through subscription and advertising, shifting value from owning recordings toward access, playlists, and recommendation.

events.label: Instagram
events.description: Instagram fuses smartphone photography, filters, profiles, followers, and a visual feed, making everyday image-making part of identity performance, influence, advertising, and platform metrics.

events.label: Twitch
events.description: Twitch makes live game play, performer commentary, audience chat, subscriptions, and donations into a participatory entertainment format built around continuous creator-audience interaction.

events.label: AlexNet and the Deep-Learning Turn
events.description: AlexNet's image-recognition performance demonstrates the power of deep neural networks trained on large datasets with GPUs, accelerating the infrastructure and methods later used by generative media.

events.label: Generative Adversarial Networks
events.description: Ian Goodfellow and collaborators introduce adversarial training between a generator and discriminator, triggering rapid advances in synthesized faces, image translation, style, and photorealism.

events.label: Neural Style Transfer
events.description: Neural style-transfer research separates and recombines learned representations of visual content and artistic style, becoming an early widely understood example of AI-assisted image transformation.

events.label: The Transformer
events.description: The Transformer architecture uses attention to model relationships across sequences efficiently at scale, becoming the foundation for large language models and many later multimodal generators.

events.label: TikTok and the Algorithmic Video Feed
events.description: Douyin and its international successor TikTok center short remixable video on a highly personalized recommendation feed, reducing the importance of an explicitly chosen social graph.

events.label: GPT-2 and Coherent Machine-Written Text
events.description: GPT-2 demonstrates that a large pretrained language model can generate extended, stylistically plausible text from a short prompt, intensifying debate over synthetic writing and release risks.

events.label: Denoising Diffusion Models
events.description: Denoising diffusion research shows that high-quality samples can be generated by learning to reverse a gradual noising process, providing the core method for the text-to-image boom.

events.label: GPT-3
events.description: GPT-3 scales language modeling to 175 billion parameters and performs many writing and reasoning tasks from instructions or examples, encouraging a market for general-purpose model APIs.

events.label: DALL-E
events.description: OpenAI's DALL-E generates novel images from natural-language descriptions, making prompt-based visual synthesis legible as a general creative interface rather than a specialist research demonstration.

events.label: GitHub Copilot
events.description: GitHub Copilot places model-generated code suggestions directly inside the editor, establishing the pattern of an AI collaborator embedded continuously within an existing creative tool.

events.label: Midjourney and Stable Diffusion
events.description: Midjourney's public service and Stable Diffusion's downloadable weights spread high-quality text-to-image generation beyond research labs, producing new aesthetics, communities, workflows, and copyright disputes.

events.label: ChatGPT
events.description: ChatGPT packages an instruction-following language model as a conversational public interface, rapidly normalizing iterative machine assistance for writing, coding, learning, brainstorming, and media production.

events.label: Adobe Firefly Enters Creative Software
events.description: Adobe integrates commercially positioned generative imaging into Photoshop and its creative ecosystem, moving generation from stand-alone novelty into established professional editing and licensing workflows.

events.label: Runway Gen-2 and Text-to-Video Production
events.description: Runway's Gen-2 makes prompt- and image-conditioned video generation available to creators, placing synthetic moving images inside an online editing and production workflow.

events.label: Video and Interactive World Models
events.description: OpenAI's Sora presents long-form video generation as learned world simulation while DeepMind's Genie generates action-controllable environments, drawing media synthesis toward dynamic models users or agents can inhabit.

events.label: Prompt-Generated Songs Become Public Tools
events.description: Services including Suno and Udio let general users generate complete songs with voices, lyrics, and arrangements from prompts, provoking adoption alongside disputes over training, style, and compensation.

events.label: From Generators to Creative Agents
events.description: Computer-use agents and model-integrated creative environments begin coordinating research, drafting, asset generation, editing, and revision across tools, reframing the model as a process collaborator rather than a single-output generator.
